reader.title: Killing of Jim Thomas
bases: A mounted party of men called a Black man out of a house at night and shot him dead, with no lawful authority and no stated motive (A2).
One unsigned paragraph in the Atlanta Constitution's state-news column is the only report found (A2).

summary.text: The killing of Jim Thomas was the shooting of a Black man by a party of mounted men on a plantation in Georgia on a Wednesday night in August 1888, most likely August 8.
The killers and their motive were unknown when the only report appeared, and no arrest or follow-up was found.
Thomas had only recently come into the neighborhood and was staying at the house of John Schley, a "colored tenant" on the plantation of Dr. L. D. Johnson.
The report described him as "apparently a quiet, harmless man" and named no county or town.
Early in the night, a party of men rode up to Schley's house and asked whether Thomas was in, and if so, for him to come out.
Thomas, "expecting no danger," answered the call, and when he came within five feet of the riders he was shot to death.
The report gives neither the number of men nor their race.
At the time of the report, who the murderers were and what their motive was were "not yet known."
No report of an inquest, arrest or trial appears in the coverage.
The killing reached print as a single unheaded paragraph in the Atlanta Constitution's weekly "Georgia News" column of August 14, 1888, which gathered items from state correspondents and exchanges.
It ran between a story about poisoned hawks in Houston County and a well accident in Dooly County.
The paragraph condemned the killing as "a foul and most dastardly murder" and a "diabolical act," while calling Thomas "the negro" and "Jim."
No report of the killing in any other paper appears in the coverage.

accounts.label: Constitution state correspondent
accounts.gist: A party of men rode up to Schley's house early on Wednesday night, asked for Thomas, and shot him dead when he came out; the killers and their motive were unknown.

framing.detail: The paragraph calls the killing 'a foul and most dastardly murder' and a 'diabolical act' and describes Thomas as quiet and harmless, without a headline of its own.

record_check.dossier: A mounted party called a Black man out at night and shot him dead without lawful authority: a completed killing by a band, best typed as a lynching, though no motive or accusation is reported.
Black: the report calls Thomas 'the negro'.
The paper prints 'Dr. L. D. Johnson'; Schley is called 'a colored tenant of Dr. Johnson'.
'Wednesday night' in a weekly column dated Tuesday, August 14; August 8 is most likely, but the column draws on weekly exchanges, so an earlier Wednesday cannot be ruled out.
Identities unknown, but described as 'a party of men' who 'rode up' to the house.
No county or town is named; neighboring items in the column concern Houston and Dooly counties, which does not place this one.

info: Wednesday night, early in the night; the column covers 'the past week', so most likely Wednesday, August 8, 1888
House of John Schley, a colored tenant, on the plantation of Dr. L. D. Johnson
Jim Thomas, called 'the negro'; recently arrived in the neighborhood
A party of men on horseback; identities unknown

sources.note: Only report: paragraph in the weekly 'Georgia News' column; party of men rode to John Schley's house on Dr. L. D. Johnson's plantation, called Jim Thomas out and shot him dead; no county or town named.
quotes: On Wednesday night a foul and most dastardly murder was committed on the plantation of Dr. L. D. Johnson.
The negro expecting no danger, answered their call, and when he got within five feet of the parties, he was shot to death.
Jim had only recently come into the neighborhood, and was apparently a quiet, harmless man.
Who were his murderers or their motive for the diabolical act are not yet known.
